title: Freezing at the doorway: a Parkinson disease visit

patient.name: Mr. Novak, 70
patient.presentation: Parkinson disease for 6 years. Freezes in doorways and on turns; two falls at home since the summer. Carbidopa-levodopa at 07:00, 11:00 and 15:00. Wants to keep walking his dog. {beltOn ? "Gait belt on." : "No gait belt on."}

rules.label: Systolic BP falls 20 mmHg or more after standing, or he feels light-headed
rules.text: Sit him down at once and recheck; tell his physician about orthostatic hypotension.

rules.label: Freezing in a doorway or turn
rules.text: Use an external cue (a line to step over, a beat to step to); never pull him forward.

objective: Parkinson disease management: aerobic exercise at moderate to high intensity, balance and gait training, external cueing for freezing, and behavior-change approaches to raise physical activity
secondaryObjectives: Measure orthostatic vital signs, recognizing orthostatic hypotension as a fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing
Monitoring and adjusting the plan of care to optimize health outcomes
Assessing, documenting and minimizing safety risks for patients and providers, including facility safety policies

brief.situation: 10:00, an outpatient neurologic clinic. Third visit for Mr. Novak, 70, with Parkinson disease. His goals: stop freezing in doorways, stop falling, keep walking his dog. Today's plan of care: aerobic work, gait training through the clinic doorway, and a home program.
handover: Last visit he froze twice at the gym doorway; you noted he 'gets stuck' when he hurries.
His wife says he has felt dizzy getting out of bed this week. His neurologist raised his carbidopa-levodopa three weeks ago.
He walks without a device. Visit length: about 45 minutes.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Tests and exercise take the time they really take; skip ahead while they run.
His heart rate and blood pressure respond to effort and standing. The stopping rules are on screen.
A written question comes early. Then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What are the two safety problems in this visit, and how does your plan answer each while still giving him the training he came for?

parts.label: Freezing
parts.criteria: Names freezing of gait at a doorway; uses an external cue (visual lines or an auditory beat) and never pulls him; guards with a gait belt; trains gait through the doorway with the cue so it carries over.
parts.modelAnswer: He freezes at doorways. An external cue, a line to step over or a beat to step to, gets him moving; pulling him makes him festinate and fall. Gait belt on, and practice the doorway with the cue.

parts.label: Orthostatic hypotension and dose
parts.criteria: Recognizes orthostatic hypotension (26/12 within 3 min) after a recent levodopa increase; stands him in stages, sits him down within seconds of light-headedness, reports it to his neurologist the same day; still gives moderate to high intensity aerobic work and a home program to raise his activity.
parts.modelAnswer: His 26/12 drop is orthostatic hypotension, likely linked to the levodopa increase: stand him in stages, especially after exercise, sit him down at once if woozy, and call his neurologist today. That is not a reason to train easy: moderate to high intensity aerobic work, gait training with cues, and a home program with a goal he sets.

scoring.modelReasoning: Two safety problems shape this visit. He freezes in doorways: an external cue, lines to step over or a beat to step to, gets him moving, while pulling him forward makes him festinate and fall; guard him with a gait belt and practice the doorway with the cue. He also has orthostatic hypotension (26/12 within 3 minutes of standing) three weeks after a carbidopa-levodopa increase: stand him in stages, especially after exercise, sit him down at once when woozy, and report it to his neurologist the same day. Neither problem is a reason to train him easy: the guideline strongly recommends moderate to high intensity aerobic exercise, balance and gait training and external cueing for freezing, and also recommends behavior-change approaches (a moderate-strength recommendation), so he leaves with a home program and a goal he sets.

choices.label: An external cue: a line to step over or a beat to step to

cueQ.explain: External cueing reduces freezing of gait (a strong recommendation); pulling or hurrying him adds to the freeze and the fall risk.
